name: Siege of Jenne (1473)
description: Sonni Ali's prolonged blockade of Jenne ending in the city's submission to Songhai.

name: Onin War
description: The ten-year war that devastated Kyoto and marked the beginning of Japan's Sengoku period.
hook: Decade-long 1467-1477 Kyoto conflict destroyed the Ashikaga shogunate and initiated Japanese feudal fragmentation.
narrative: The Onin War erupted from succession disputes within the Ashikaga shogunate, with two factions competing for the shogun's position. The conflict centered on Kyoto but devastated the capital and triggered the rise of independent daimyo. The war, ostensibly between the Yamana and Ōuchi clans, devolved into decades of feudal conflict. The Ashikaga shogunate's authority never recovered after Onin's conclusion. The period initiated the Sengoku ('Warring States') era of feudal fragmentation.
significance: The Onin War destroyed Japan's remaining centralized authority and initiated two centuries of feudal warfare. The destruction of Kyoto demonstrated military dominance's shift from court nobility to armed daimyo. The war's aftermath presaged the complete restructuring of Japanese political organization.

name: Sengoku Period (Japan)
description: The period of civil war in Japan between feudal daimyo that ended with unification under the Tokugawa.
hook: A century of Japanese warlord warfare created the conditions for national unification and samurai dominance.
narrative: The Sengoku Period (1467-1615) saw Japan fragment into competing domains (daimyo) fighting for supremacy. Major power centers included the Takeda, Uesugi, Imagawa, Oda, Toyotomi, and Tokugawa clans. Innovations included early firearms (introduced 1543), castle warfare, and conscripted peasant armies. Three towering figures emerged: Oda Nobunaga (1534-1582), who unified much of Japan; Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1537-1598), who completed unification; and Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543-1616), who established a dynasty. Famous battles included Sekigahara (1600), where Tokugawa defeated the Toyotomi. The period's warfare was brutal, involving sieges and mass casualties.
significance: The Sengoku wars unified Japan politically and militarily. The Tokugawa Shogunate (1603-1868) provided unprecedented stability and isolation. The period elevated the samurai class and established bushido (the warrior code). The adoption of firearms transformed Japanese warfare. The period's unification created the conditions for Japan's rapid modernization in the 19th century.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Sengoku Period - Warring States Japan
description: Nearly 150 years of fragmented warfare between Japanese feudal lords (daimyo) saw the rise of powerful warlords who gradually unified Japan. The period ended with the establishment of the Tokugawa shogunate and lasting peace.
hook: Japanese feudal lords (daimyo) waged unceasing warfare, creating a martial culture that unified the nation.
narrative: The Sengoku Period (1467-1615) saw Japan fragment into competing domains ruled by daimyo. The period began with the Onin War (1467-1477), which destroyed the Ashikaga shogunate's authority. Thereafter, daimyo fought constantly for territorial expansion and supremacy. Key military innovations included the adoption of firearms (introduced 1543) and changes in castle architecture to resist cannon fire. Three powerful daimyo eventually emerged: Oda Nobunaga (conquered much of central Japan), Toyotomi Hideyoshi (completed unification), and Tokugawa Ieyasu (established a stable shogunate). The period's warfare was characterized by large armies, complex logistics, and tactical innovation.
significance: The Sengoku wars unified Japan politically and militarily under the Tokugawa Shogunate, ushering in 250 years of stability. The period elevated the samurai class to dominance and established bushido (the warrior code). The period's military innovations influenced East Asian warfare. The unification created the conditions for Japan's rapid modernization in the 19th century and its emergence as a major Asian power.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Sengoku Period - Warring States Japan
Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Songhai Conquest of Timbuktu
description: Askia Muhammad's conquest of Timbuktu and consolidation of Songhai control over Mali.
hook: Songhai conquest of Timbuktu secured control of West Africa's major Islamic and commercial center.
narrative: Timbuktu, a major Islamic learning center and trade hub, fell to Songhai military conquest. The conquest gave Songhai control of critical intellectual and commercial resources. Songhai maintained Timbuktu's Islamic institutions.
significance: Timbuktu conquest consolidated Songhai dominance and demonstrated Songhai respect for Islamic learning.

name: Songhai Empire Expansion
description: Songhai Empire's expansion becoming the dominant West African power.
hook: Songhai Dynasty expanded territorial control across West Africa under successive emperors.
narrative: Songhai expansion under Ali and Askia incorporated vast West African territories. Military campaigns conquered rival powers and integrated them into tributary systems. Songhai military organization included professional cavalry and administrative structures.
significance: Songhai expansion created West Africa's largest pre-colonial state. The empire's administrative innovations influenced successor states.

name: Aztec-Tarascan Wars
description: Series of Aztec military campaigns to subdue the rival Tarascan Empire in Michoacán. The Aztecs were repulsed at Tzintzuntzan, establishing a disputed western border that neither power could decisively cross.

name: Inca Conquest of Chimú
description: Topa Inca's conquest of the Chimú Kingdom, adding the northern coast to Inca territory. This was the largest territorial acquisition of the later Inca expansion phase.
hook: Inca conquest of the Chimú Empire established Inca hegemony over Peruvian coastal regions.
narrative: The Chimú Empire, a major coastal power, controlled advanced irrigation systems and wealthy coastal territories. Inca forces, under Topa Inca or Pachacuti, conducted systematic conquest of Chimú territories. Chimú military resistance crumbled before Inca organization. The conquest integrated Chimú administrative expertise into Inca systems.
significance: Inca conquest of the Chimú established Inca dominance over coastal regions and integrated critical irrigation technology. The Chimú's administrative knowledge influenced Inca imperial organization.

name: Inca-Chimor Conquest
description: Inca conquest of Chimor, the largest pre-Inca civilization.
hook: Inca expansion incorporated the Chimor Empire and its coastal territories into the Inca realm.
narrative: The Inca conquest of Chimor (Chimú Empire) represented a major imperial expansion. Chimor's wealth and administrative sophistication made it a significant prize. Military campaigns reduced Chimor resistance. The conquest demonstrated Inca ability to assimilate complex coastal societies.
significance: Chimor conquest established Inca coastal control and integrated sophisticated Chimor administrative systems. The victory demonstrated Inca imperial capacity.

name: Mai Ali Ghaji's Restoration of Bornu
description: Mai Ali Ghaji ibn Dunama's campaigns founding the new Bornu capital at Ngazargamu and restoring Sefuwa power over the Bulala.

name: Cham–Vietnamese War (1471)
description: Lê Thánh Tông's sack of Vijaya effectively destroyed Champa as a major polity.

name: Topa Inca's Expansion Wars
description: Extensive campaigns by Topa Inca to expand Inca territory south into modern Chile and Argentina, and east into the Amazon basin. Doubled the empire's territorial extent.
hook: Topa Inca's military campaigns expanded the Inca Empire into Ecuador and Chile (1471-1493).
narrative: Topa Inca succeeded Pachacuti and continued imperial expansion. His campaigns conquered northern Ecuador territories and extended Inca control southward into Chile. Northern expansion incorporated new ethnic groups and established Inca administrative control over vast new territories.
significance: Topa Inca's expansion achieved Inca hegemony over unprecedented Andean territories. The expanded empire created the imperial state confronting Spanish conquest.

name: Diaguita Resistance to Inca Conquest
description: Ongoing Inca military campaigns to subdue the Diaguita peoples of northwestern Argentina and Chile. Diaguita resistance persisted throughout the Inca occupation until Spanish conquest.
hook: Diaguita people resisted Inca expansion in northwestern Argentina before Spanish colonization.
narrative: The Diaguita, living in northwestern Argentina, resisted Inca conquest through guerrilla warfare and fortified settlement defense. Despite Inca military superiority, Diaguita warriors maintained resistance across generations. Inca ultimately incorporated Diaguita territories but Diaguita culture persisted.
significance: Diaguita resistance demonstrated that Inca conquest was not inevitable and required sustained military effort. Diaguita cultural resilience influenced Andean colonial development.

name: Muscovite-Novgorod Wars
description: Muscovite conquest of Novgorod establishing Moscow dominance.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Crimea
description: Ottoman forces conquered Crimea from Genoese and local rulers, establishing a Crimean Khanate as an Ottoman vassal. This conquest gave the Ottomans control of the Black Sea coast.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Moldavia
description: Ottoman forces conquered Moldavia, completing Ottoman conquest of the Balkans and establishing Ottoman control of the Danube region. Moldavia became an Ottoman vassal state like Wallachia.

name: Sengoku Period Conflicts
description: Prolonged period of warfare between feudal lords (daimyo) with famous battles at Sekigahara and other sites.
hook: Japan's Sengoku warfare created a martial culture and military tradition that dominated East Asia for centuries.
narrative: The Sengoku Period (1467-1615) was characterized by constant warfare among daimyo (feudal lords) seeking territorial expansion. Armies grew from samurai-dominated forces to include conscripted peasants with firearms. Castles became increasingly sophisticated, driving innovations in fortification. Major campaigns included the Takeda-Uesugi rivalry (Kawanakajima battles), Oda Nobunaga's unification wars (defeating the Imagawa and Uesugi), and Toyotomi Hideyoshi's subjugation of remaining daimyo (siege of Odawara, 1590). The period's warfare was marked by rapid tactical evolution, from traditional samurai mounted combat to pike-and-shot infantry formations. By 1600, the Tokugawa Shogunate defeated the Toyotomi at Sekigahara, establishing a unified state.
significance: The Sengoku wars created a unified Japanese state under the Tokugawa Shogunate, enabling nearly 300 years of stability and prosperity. The period established Japanese military traditions (castle architecture, samurai codes) that persisted until modernization. The wars demonstrated the superiority of organized firearms over traditional samurai tactics. Japan's unification positioned it to resist European colonization and modernize rapidly in the 19th century.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Ottoman Conquest of Albania
description: Ottoman forces conquered Albania from Venice after a prolonged siege of Shkoder, establishing Ottoman control of the western Balkans. Albania remained Ottoman for over 400 years.

name: Songhai Gao Expansion
description: Songhai expansion from Gao as a major West African imperial power.
hook: Songhai expansion extended hegemony over Gao and adjacent Niger River valley territories.
narrative: Gao, another major West African commercial center, fell to Songhai military campaigns. Gao's conquest completed Songhai control over critical Niger valley trade routes.
significance: Gao conquest solidified Songhai regional dominance and trade network control.

name: Decline of the Golden Horde
description: The fragmented remains of the Mongol Golden Horde were conquered or became vassals of the emerging Russian state and Ottoman Empire. This process marked the end of Mongol dominance in Eastern Europe.

name: Conquest of Granada
description: The final campaign of the Reconquista that conquered the last Islamic emirate in Iberia.

name: Reconquista - Granada War
description: The final campaign of the Reconquista saw Catholic monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella conquer the last Muslim state in Iberia. This victory consolidated Spanish Christian power and freed resources for overseas expansion.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Herzegovina
description: Ottoman forces conquered Herzegovina, completing Ottoman control of the southern Balkans. Herzegovina became an Ottoman province for centuries.

name: Moldavian-Ottoman Wars
description: The prolonged conflicts between Moldavia and the Ottoman Empire for control of the region.

name: Battle of Bosworth Field
description: Henry VII's victory that ended the Wars of the Roses and established the Tudor dynasty.

name: Aztec Conquest of Soconusco
description: Aztec military campaign under Ahuitzotl to conquer the wealthy Soconusco region on the southern Pacific coast, bringing valuable tribute including cacao.
hook: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire exploited internal divisions, indigenous allies, and epidemic disease.
narrative: Hernán Cortés arrived at Tenochtitlan in 1519 with 600 men, capturing Emperor Montezuma II as hostage. Montezuma's death and Cortés's retreat in the Night of Sorrows (June 1520) preceded Cortés's return with Tlaxcalan allies. Epidemic smallpox devastated the Aztec capital. The 93-day Siege of Tenochtitlan (May-August 1521) methodically starved the city. Cuauhtémoc's capture in August 1521 ended organized resistance.
significance: Aztec collapse within two years—facilitated by disease, indigenous alliances, and Spanish firepower—triggered Spanish America's foundation. The conquest introduced European infectious diseases killing millions.

name: Aztec Conquest of the Huasteca
description: Aztec conquest of the Huasteca region by Ahuitzotl, bringing the northern Gulf coast under Aztec tribute control.
hook: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire exploited internal divisions, indigenous allies, and epidemic disease.
narrative: Hernán Cortés arrived at Tenochtitlan in 1519 with 600 men, capturing Emperor Montezuma II as hostage. Montezuma's death and Cortés's retreat in the Night of Sorrows (June 1520) preceded Cortés's return with Tlaxcalan allies. Epidemic smallpox devastated the Aztec capital. The 93-day Siege of Tenochtitlan (May-August 1521) methodically starved the city. Cuauhtémoc's capture in August 1521 ended organized resistance.
significance: Aztec collapse within two years—facilitated by disease, indigenous alliances, and Spanish firepower—triggered Spanish America's foundation. The conquest introduced European infectious diseases killing millions.

name: Ikko-Ikki Rebellions
description: Repeated rebellions by Buddhist-led peasant armies against feudal lords.

name: Ottoman-Venetian Trade Wars
description: A series of conflicts between Venice and the Ottoman Empire over trade routes and Mediterranean territories resulted in Venetian loss of dominance. Ottoman control of Mediterranean trade increased significantly.

name: Mahfuz's jihads
description: Emir Mahfuz of Harar's annual Lenten jihads against Ethiopia, killed by Lebna Dengel in 1517, foreshadowed Gragn's wars.

name: Columbus Expeditions and Early Contact
description: Columbus's four voyages to the Caribbean and introduction of European conquest. Initiated the catastrophic Columbian Exchange affecting all subsequent American history.

name: Columbus Expeditions to the Americas
description: Christopher Columbus's expeditions initiated European contact with the Americas, leading to massive displacement and death of indigenous populations through conquest and disease. These voyages fundamentally reshaped world history and began Spanish colonial dominance in the Western Hemisphere.

name: Portuguese-Spanish Colonial Rivalry
description: Spain and Portugal divided the Americas through treaties and conflicts, with Spain dominating the majority. The division created the basis for modern Spanish and Portuguese-speaking Americas.
hook: Portugal and Spain competed to build global colonial empires, dividing the world between them.
narrative: Portuguese and Spanish colonial rivalry (15th-18th centuries) shaped the global colonial system. Portugal, under Prince Henry the Navigator, pioneered ocean exploration and established trading posts along African coasts (1400s) and eventually reached India (Vasco da Gama, 1498). Spain, after supporting Columbus's expedition (1492), established colonies in the Americas. The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided the non-European world between Portugal and Spain. Portugal controlled territories in Africa, India, and Asia (Goa, Malacca, Brazil). Spain controlled most of the Americas. Competition erupted in the Pacific (the Philippines) and occasionally in military clashes (Battle of Diu, 1509). Both powers relied on superior naval technology and military superiority over indigenous peoples.
significance: Portuguese and Spanish colonial rivalry established the template for European colonialism and the global colonial system. The two nations' dominance in colonial ventures lasted until the 17th century, when the Dutch and English challenged their monopolies. The colonial competition resulted in the exploitation and decimation of indigenous populations, the transatlantic slave trade, and the transfer of vast wealth to Europe. The colonial empires shaped modern global inequalities and international relations. The legacy of Iberian colonialism persists in the cultural, linguistic, and religious identities of Latin America, Africa, and Asia.

name: Huayna Capac's Northern Campaigns
description: Inca expansion campaigns into Ecuador and the north. Huayna Capac extended Inca territory to modern Colombia while facing resistance.

name: Askia Muhammad's Wars
description: Askia Muhammad I's campaigns extending Songhai control over Air, Hausaland, the Mossi, and Diara, including the 1497–98 jihad against the Mossi.

name: First Italian War
description: French King Charles VIII invaded Italy, initiating a series of conflicts over Italian territory that would span six decades. This war established the pattern of European powers competing for control of the Italian peninsula.

name: Italian Wars
description: The prolonged conflicts between Spain and France for control of Italy and its territories.
hook: European powers contended for control of Italy through military campaigns and dynastic diplomacy (1494-1559).
narrative: The Italian Wars pitted French kings against Spanish Habsburgs for dominance over Italian territories. The wars began with Charles VIII of France's invasion of Naples in 1494. Subsequent campaigns involved shifting alliances, papal involvement, and mercenary forces. Major battles included Marignano (1515, French victory), Pavia (1525, Spanish capture of Francis I), and the sack of Rome (1527, Spanish troops). The wars devastated Italian city-states and demonstrated the emerging power of centralized nation-states over Italian republican structures. The Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis (1559) established Spanish dominance over much of Italy.
significance: Italian Wars demonstrated the vulnerability of city-states to centralized national powers. The conflicts ended Italian independence and initiated Spanish-Habsburg dominance. The wars presaged the modern state system's emergence over medieval feudalism.

name: Third Italian War
description: A series of conflicts over Italian territory concluded with Spanish dominance and the Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis, which established Spain as the major European power. These wars reshaped European political geography.

name: Spanish Conquest of Melilla
description: Castilian seizure of Melilla under Pedro de Estopiñán, beginning Spanish Plazas de Soberanía on the Moroccan coast.

name: Fourth Ottoman-Venetian War
description: Ottoman-Venetian naval war in Mediterranean, resulting in Ottoman territorial gains.

name: Venetian-Ottoman War
description: The Ottoman Navy defeated Venice in several naval engagements, establishing Ottoman naval dominance in the Mediterranean. Venice lost key territories including Greek possessions.

name: Second Italian War
description: France and Spain competed for control of Milan and Naples, with Spain ultimately establishing dominance in southern Italy. This war consolidated Spanish power in the Mediterranean.

name: Bruneian conquest of Manila
description: Brunei extended its empire over Manila Bay in the late 15th century.

name: Funj Conquest of Alodia
description: Funj founder Amara Dunqas's destruction of the Christian Nubian kingdom of Alodia and foundation of the Sennar Sultanate.

name: Songhai Conquest of Air
description: Askia Muhammad's conquest of Agadez and the Aïr massif.

name: Aztec Tributary Uprisings
description: Periodic rebellions by tributary states against Aztec dominance. These revolts weakened empire cohesion and demonstrated resentment of Aztec rule.

name: Incan Provincial Revolts
description: Various provincial uprisings against Inca imperial rule in the decades before Spanish conquest. Demonstrated imperial vulnerability to internal revolt.
hook: Subject populations within the Inca Empire periodically rebelled against Inca tribute and rule.
narrative: Despite Inca administrative sophistication, subject peoples occasionally revolted against Inca control. Regional rebellions involved military campaigns to suppress resistance. Inca military response demonstrated imperial capacity to maintain dominance. Revolts provided opportunities for rival Inca factions to compete for imperial power.
significance: Provincial revolts demonstrated that Inca rule depended on military enforcement. The revolts created vulnerabilities exploitable during Spanish conquest.

name: Portuguese Expansion in Africa
description: Portuguese explorers and traders established coastal fortresses and trading posts across Africa, beginning European colonization of the continent. Portuguese naval superiority allowed them to dominate African coastal trade for two centuries.

name: Ottoman-Hungarian Wars
description: A century of warfare between the Ottomans and Hungary resulted in Ottoman conquest of much of Hungary. These conflicts lasted until the Treaty of Zsitvatorok in 1606.

casualtyRange.notes: 1500-1606. Multiple conflicts and sieges. Ottoman expansion into Hungary.

hook: Ottoman expansion collided with Hungarian resistance, reshaping the balance of power in Southeast Europe.
narrative: The Ottoman Empire's expansion into Southeast Europe (15th-16th centuries) brought it into conflict with Hungary, a major Christian kingdom. The Ottoman-Hungarian Wars included multiple campaigns and devastating Ottoman victories. The Battle of Mohács (1526) was a catastrophic Hungarian defeat that left the kingdom divided and Ottoman-dominated. Ottoman forces advanced toward Vienna but were halted at the Gates of Vienna (1529). Successive Ottoman-Hungarian conflicts (16th-17th centuries) saw the Ottomans gradually advance westward. The Ottoman conquest of Hungary demonstrated superior military organization, logistics, and the effectiveness of Ottoman janissaries (elite infantry) and cavalry.
significance: The Ottoman-Hungarian Wars established Ottoman dominance in Southeast Europe and blocked further westward expansion. The wars prevented Ottoman conquest of Central Europe (though Vienna was threatened). The conflicts demonstrated the resilience of Christian kingdoms against Ottoman advance. The wars' outcome reshaped the balance of power between the Ottoman and European worlds. The conflicts influenced European perceptions of the Ottoman threat and motivated Christian unity efforts.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Powhatan-Monacan Wars
description: Territorial conflicts between the powerful Powhatan Confederacy and the Monacan peoples of the Virginia Piedmont. Powhatan dominance was established by the time of European settlement.

name: Benin-Yoruba Conflicts
description: Territorial and commercial conflicts between Benin and neighboring Yoruba city-states.

name: Ottoman-Circassian Wars
description: Ottoman conflicts with Caucasian peoples including Circassians resulted in massive depopulation and displacement. Ottoman control of the Caucasus remained contested against local resistance.

name: Ottoman-Georgian Wars
description: Georgian kingdoms faced pressure from both Ottoman and Persian powers, gradually coming under Ottoman and Russian influence. Georgia became a contested borderland between empires.

name: Spanish Expansion in North Africa
description: Spanish forces conquered several North African coastal enclaves and fought Ottoman and Moroccan forces for regional dominance. Spanish control remained limited to small coastal areas.

name: Vietnamese Expansion South - Nam Vu
description: Vietnamese states gradually conquered the Kingdom of Champa and expanded southward into the Mekong Delta, creating modern Vietnam's territorial extent. This expansion displaced numerous Southeast Asian populations and established Vietnamese dominance in Indochina.

name: Polish-Ottoman Conflicts
description: Centuries of conflicts between Poland-Lithuania and the Ottoman Empire over territorial control of Eastern Europe and the Balkans resulted in Ottoman expansion to Europe. Poland ultimately declined as Ottoman power waned.

name: Brazilian Indigenous Resistance to Portuguese
description: Centuries-long indigenous resistance to Portuguese colonial expansion. Tupi, Guaraní, and other groups resisted Portuguese settlement and enslavement.

name: Portuguese Conquest of Brazil
description: Portuguese conquistadors and settlers gradually conquered Brazil from indigenous peoples and competing European powers, establishing Portugal's largest and most valuable colony. The conquest devastated indigenous populations through warfare and disease.
hook: Portugal colonized Brazil through gradual settlement, indigenous enslavement, and transplantation of African slaves.
narrative: After Pedro Álvares Cabral landed in 1500, Portugal slowly established trading posts and colonies along Brazil's coast. Initial indigenous resistance (Tupí, Guató, and other groups) impeded early settlement. By the 1530s, the crown granted hereditary captaincies to encourage colonization. Portuguese settlers enslaved indigenous peoples for labor; when disease and flight depleted this workforce, they turned to the transatlantic slave trade (beginning 1538). Competition with the French spurred Portuguese expansion inland. Key developments included the founding of Rio de Janeiro (1565) and São Paulo (1554), and conflicts with rival European powers for colonial dominance. By 1750, Portugal controlled much of the continent.
significance: Brazil became the world's largest slave society, importing 4.9 million enslaved Africans—more than any other destination. This created a mixed-race, plantation-based colonial society fundamentally different from Spanish America. Brazil's racial demographics and social structure were forged through this conquest and enslavement. The conflict established Portugal as a major Atlantic power.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Burmese-Mon Wars
description: Burmese forces gradually conquered and absorbed the Mon Kingdom, extending Burmese rule over lower Burma. This conquest created the modern extent of Burmese territory.
hook: Pyu, Mon, and Burman peoples competed for dominance over Burma through military conquest (6th-18th centuries).
narrative: The Pyu, an early Sino-Tibetan people, dominated central Burma until Burman migrations (9th-10th centuries) and the later Shan invasions. The Mon Kingdom controlled lower Burma from ancient times. Various Burman dynasties (Pagan, Ava, Toungoo, Konbaung) fought to control Mon territories and unify the region. Anawrahta of Pagan (1044-1077) unified much of Burma by conquering the Mon kingdom, establishing Pagan as a regional superpower. Subsequent dynasties continuously fought Mon resistance and Thai pressure. By the 18th century, the Konbaung Dynasty consolidated Burman control, but Mon cultural identity persisted.
significance: Burman-Mon conflicts established Burman political dominance despite Mon cultural significance. The unification process under successive dynasties created the Burmese state structure. Mon cultural traditions influenced Burmese art, religion, and governance.

name: French-Spanish Colonial Wars
description: Centuries of conflict between France and Spain over colonial territories in North America and the Caribbean resulted in gradual French expansion. The conflicts concluded with British dominance in North America.

name: Russian-Polish Conflicts
description: Centuries of conflicts between Russia and Poland-Lithuania over Eastern Europe resulted in Polish decline and Russian expansion. Russia ultimately partitioned Poland by 1795.
hook: Centuries of warfare between Russia and Poland determined control of Eastern Europe and shaped regional geopolitics.
narrative: Russian-Polish conflicts (14th-18th centuries) were recurrent struggles for dominance in Eastern Europe. Early conflicts included the Teutonic Order, Polish, and Russian competition in the region. Major wars included Poland-Lithuania's rise to power (16th-17th centuries) and subsequent Russian expansion. The Russo-Polish War (1654-1667) saw Russia conquer significant Polish-Lithuanian territories. Peter the Great's wars against Sweden (Great Northern War) also involved Polish territories. By the late 18th century, Russia had become the dominant power, and through the Partitions of Poland (1772, 1793, 1795), Russia, Prussia, and Austria divided Poland among themselves. The conflicts drove Polish partition and subjugation until Polish independence (1918).
significance: Russian-Polish conflicts established Russia as the dominant Eastern European power and facilitated the partitions of Poland. The conflicts' outcome left Poland divided and subjugated until the 20th century. The wars influenced Polish national identity and resistance to Russian rule. Polish-Russian tensions persisted into the modern era, shaping Cold War politics and contemporary European tensions. The conflicts demonstrated the vulnerability of intermediate powers to pressure from stronger neighbors.

name: American Indian Wars
description: Three centuries of conflict between European colonists and Native American peoples resulted in the near-total displacement of Native Americans. These wars transformed North American demographics and geography.
hook: Three centuries of indigenous resistance against European colonization fundamentally reshaped the Americas.
narrative: From the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire (1519-1521) through the North American Indian Wars (1607-1890s), indigenous peoples fought colonizers across the continents. Initial Spanish conquests employed superior weaponry, disease, and alliances with indigenous rivals. North American conflicts saw tribes alternately ally with European powers (French, British) and adapt militarily—from mounted warfare on the Great Plains to ambush tactics in forests. Key moments included King Philip's War (1675), the Pueblo Revolt (1680), Tecumseh's Confederacy (1809), and the Great Sioux Wars (1876). The U.S. Army's systematic campaigns in the 1880s-1890s (Wounded Knee, Apache Wars) marked colonization's final phase.
significance: The wars resulted in the near-complete removal or displacement of indigenous peoples, the seizure of their lands, and the suppression of their sovereignty. Disease killed far more than warfare. The conflicts shaped the territorial expansion and ethnic composition of the United States and Canada. Contemporary indigenous rights movements trace their origins to this period of dispossession.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Benin–Itsekiri Wars
description: Wars between Benin and its breakaway Itsekiri kingdom of Warri.

name: Cambodian-Thai Wars
description: Conflicts between Cambodia and Siam resulted in Thai expansion and Cambodian contraction, reducing Cambodia to a vassal state. These wars reshaped Southeast Asian power dynamics.

name: Hausa-Fulani Conflicts
description: Territorial and cultural conflicts between Hausa city-states and Fulani pastoralists.

name: Safavid Empire Formation
description: The Safavid Dynasty conquered Persia, establishing Shia Islam as the state religion and creating a major Islamic empire. The Safavids rivaled the Ottomans for centuries as the dominant Middle Eastern power.
hook: Shiite militant movement conquered Persia, establishing the Safavid Empire as Islam's major Shiite power.
narrative: The Safavid movement, founded by Safi al-Din Ardabili, began as a Sufi mystical order but transformed into a militant political force. Under Ismail I (r. 1501-1524), the Safavids conquered Persia (modern-day Iran) through a series of military campaigns. Ismail's forces, fired by religious zeal, defeated rival dynasties (Aq Qoyunlu, various local lords) and established Shiite Islam as the state religion. The conquest of Persia created a major Shiite power rivaling the Sunni Ottoman Empire. Subsequent Safavid rulers (Tahmasp, Abbas) expanded the empire, developing sophisticated administrative systems and military technology. The Safavids became a major regional power.
significance: The Safavid formation established Persia as a Shiite-majority nation, a status that persists to the present day. The establishment of Shiism as the state religion created a permanent religious divide between the Safavid and Ottoman empires. The Safavid Empire became a major center of Islamic culture and learning. The empire's formation reshaped Middle Eastern geopolitics, creating a tri-polar balance (Ottomans, Safavids, European powers). The Safavid legacy influenced modern Iran's political and religious identity.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Portuguese sack of Kilwa (1505)
description: Almeida built the Gereza fort and installed a Portuguese puppet sultan at Kilwa, beginning Lusitanian rule on the Swahili coast.

name: Portuguese sack of Mombasa (1505)
description: Francisco de Almeida's fleet stormed and burned Mombasa on the first Portuguese reconnaissance of the Swahili coast.

name: Portuguese Conquest of Mozambique
description: Portuguese forces conquered Mozambique from Arab traders and Swahili states, establishing Portuguese control of the southeastern African coast. Portuguese rule lasted until the 20th century.

name: Portuguese Expansion in India
description: Portuguese forces conquered Goa and other Indian ports, establishing a Portuguese maritime empire in the Indian Ocean. Portuguese dominance of Indian Ocean trade lasted until challenged by the Dutch and British.

name: Portuguese-Swahili Conflicts
description: Conflicts over control of East African trade routes between Portuguese colonizers and Swahili traders.

name: Kongo Civil War of 1506
description: Succession war in which the Christian prince Mvemba a Nzinga (Afonso I) defeated his pagan half-brother Mpanzu a Kitima at the Battle of Mbanza Kongo, securing the throne and the Portuguese alliance.

name: Kongo-Portuguese Conflicts
description: Long conflict between Portuguese colonial ambitions and the Kingdom of Kongo.
hook: Portuguese intervention in Kongo Kingdom politics escalated internal conflicts and undermined centralization.
narrative: Portuguese involvement in Kongo political conflicts amplified internal factional disputes. Portuguese supported rival claimants to the Kongo throne. The conflicts fragmented Kongo politically and enabled Portuguese exploitation.
significance: Portuguese intervention weaponized Kongo internal divisions. The conflict presaged European colonialism through internal division exploitation.

name: Spanish Conquest of Oran
description: Cardinal Cisneros's expedition capturing Oran, part of the Spanish offensive into the Maghreb after the fall of Granada.

name: Portuguese-Ottoman Conflicts in Indian Ocean
description: Portuguese naval forces competed with Ottoman and Arab powers for control of Indian Ocean trade routes, establishing Portuguese naval dominance. Though eventually challenged by other European powers, Portugal maintained regional influence for centuries.

name: Portuguese Conquest of Goa
description: Portuguese forces under Afonso de Albuquerque conquered the strategic port city of Goa, establishing a major Portuguese colonial center in India. Goa served as the capital of Portuguese India for centuries.
hook: 1510 Portuguese conquest of Goa established European presence in Indian Ocean.
narrative: Portuguese forces under Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate in 1510. The conquest involved naval operations and assault on fortified positions. Goa became the center of Portuguese Indian Ocean empire.
significance: Goa's conquest established Portuguese foothold in India. The city became the administrative center for Portuguese Asian expansion.

name: Toungoo Dynasty Expansion
description: Toungoo's expansion creating Burmese hegemony.

name: Capture of Malacca (1511)
description: Afonso de Albuquerque seized Malacca, beginning European naval primacy in Southeast Asia.

name: Portuguese Spice Wars in Moluccas
description: Portuguese traders and soldiers fought to monopolize the spice trade in the Moluccas, establishing fortified trading posts. Portuguese control gradually declined as the Dutch and British challenged their dominance.

name: Portuguese Conquest of the Spice Islands
description: Portuguese traders and soldiers fought to monopolize spice trade in the Moluccas, establishing fortified trading posts before being displaced by the Dutch. The Moluccas became the source of Europe's spice wealth.

name: Battle of Flodden
description: The English victory against Scotland that killed King James IV and many Scottish nobles.

name: Battle of Chaldiran
description: Ottoman forces decisively defeated the Safavid Empire, establishing Ottoman control over Mesopotamia and much of the Caucasus. This battle marked the beginning of centuries of Ottoman-Persian rivalry.

name: Kebbi–Songhai War
description: Kanta Kotal's revolt against Askia Muhammad founded the kingdom of Kebbi and broke Songhai control of Hausaland's western marches.

name: Ottoman-Mamluk War
description: Ottoman forces decisively defeated the Mamluk Sultanate, conquering Egypt and the Levant and establishing Ottoman hegemony in the eastern Mediterranean. This victory made the Ottomans the dominant Islamic power.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Algiers
description: Ottoman forces took control of Algiers, establishing Ottoman dominance over the Barbary States of North Africa. Algiers became a major Ottoman naval base for the next 300 years.

name: Ottoman Conquest of North Africa
description: Ottoman forces and Barbary corsairs conquered North African territories from Spain and established Ottoman dominance. The Barbary States became autonomous Ottoman provinces.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Mecca and Medina
description: Ottoman forces conquered the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina from the Mamluks, establishing Ottoman control and prestige. The Ottomans became recognized as protectors of Islam.

name: Fall of Majapahit
description: Demak's destruction of the last Majapahit court at Daha around 1527.

name: Johor–Portuguese wars
description: Century-long Johor effort to reclaim Malacca from Portugal.

name: Spanish Conquest of Mexico
description: Hernán Cortés led a relatively small Spanish force that conquered the massive Aztec Empire, largely through exploitation of indigenous rivalries and disease. This conquest established Spanish control over Mesoamerica and resulted in catastrophic population decline.

casualtyRange.source: Wikipedia: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire; Clodfelter
casualtyRange.notes: Conquest 1519-1521 + aftermath. Direct combat lower; most deaths from disease and famine post-conquest.

hook: Spanish conquest of Mexico (1519-1521) destroyed indigenous civilizations and created New Spain—the foundation of modern Mexico.
narrative: Cortés' conquest of Mexico (1519-1521) as described above. Following conquest, Spain established New Spain colonial rule (1521-1821). Spanish imposed Christianity, Spanish language, and racial hierarchy. Indigenous populations were enslaved in encomienda system. Mestizaje created mixed-race population. Spanish extracted wealth (silver, agriculture, labor) for 300 years. By 1821, Mexican independence created a new nation inheriting Spanish colonial structures and inequalities.
significance: Spanish conquest transformed Mexico from indigenous empires to European colonial state. It created Mexican mestizo identity and Spanish-speaking Catholic civilization. Colonial extraction enriched Spain and Europe; Mexico inherited poverty and inequality. The conquest's legacy—colonial structures, racial hierarchy, indigenous marginalization—shapes modern Mexico. Modern Mexican nationalism partly invokes indigenous resistance to Spanish conquest while accepting mestizaje as defining identity.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Spanish Conquest of the Aztec Empire
description: Hernán Cortés led Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire, resulting in the fall of Tenochtitlan and Spanish dominion over Mexico.

casualtyRange.source: Wikipedia: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire; Clodfelter
casualtyRange.notes: Conquest 1519-1521 + aftermath. Direct combat lower; most deaths from disease and famine post-conquest.

hook: Cortés' 600 men, indigenous allies, and smallpox toppled the Aztec Empire—killing millions through conquest and disease.
narrative: Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico (1519) seeking gold. The Aztec Empire under Montezuma II seemed invincible: 100,000-strong capital Tenochtitlan, millions of subjects, and sophisticated warfare. Cortés exploited indigenous resentment of Aztec tributary demands, recruited tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan and other allied warriors, and besieged Tenochtitlan (1520-1521). Smallpox decimated the population mid-siege. The Aztec surrendered; Cortés razed the city. Conquest killed soldiers and civilians through violence; smallpox killed millions in the following decades as European diseases swept Mesoamerica.
significance: Spanish conquest ended Aztec civilization and initiated 300 years of Spanish colonial rule in Mexico. Disease killed more indigenous people than the sword—90% population collapse across Mesoamerica. The conquest redistributed wealth to Spain, funding European Wars for 200 years. It marked the beginning of European global dominance and the end of indigenous American political autonomy. Mestizaje (mixing) and cultural hybridity emerged. Modern Mexico's identity is rooted in this collision.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Spanish Conquest of Northern Mexico
description: Spanish expansion into northern Mexico against fierce indigenous resistance. Slow and difficult conquest of nomadic and semi-nomadic peoples.

name: Portuguese Conquest of East Timor
description: Portuguese explorers and traders gradually conquered East Timor through military campaigns and diplomacy, establishing Portuguese colonial control. Portuguese rule lasted until the 20th century.

name: Battle of Mactan
description: Lapulapu's warriors killed Magellan in 1521.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Belgrade
description: Ottoman forces captured Belgrade from Hungary, establishing Ottoman control of the Danube region. This conquest opened the way for further Ottoman advances into Central Europe.

name: Italian Wars - Franco-Spanish Conflicts
description: A series of devastating wars between France and the Spanish-controlled Holy Roman Empire over control of Italian territories and European hegemony. These conflicts transformed European diplomacy and military tactics.
hook: 16th-century wars between France and Spain for control of Italy reshaped European power balances.
narrative: The Italian Wars (1494-1559) were a series of conflicts between France and Spain, with other European powers intervening, for control of Italian territories. The wars began with French King Charles VIII's invasion of Italy (1494) to claim the Kingdom of Naples. Subsequent French-Spanish conflicts involved Sicily, Milan, and Naples. Major battles included Pavia (1525), where Spain decisively defeated France. The wars were characterized by shifting alliances, mercenary armies, and the use of advancing military technology (firearms, artillery, fortifications). The wars devastated Italy economically and politically. The Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis (1559) settled the conflicts, with Spain gaining dominance over Italian territories.
significance: The Italian Wars demonstrated the vulnerability of Italian city-states to external invasion by consolidated European powers. The wars' outcome established Spain as a dominant European power and French power's limitations in Italy. The wars accelerated the decline of Italian city-state independence and contributed to Italy's political fragmentation until the 19th century. The conflicts influenced European military tactics and fortification designs. The wars' costs demonstrated the economic burden of warfare on European treasuries.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Ottoman Conquest of Rhodes
description: Ottoman forces conquered Rhodes from the Knights Hospitaller, extending Ottoman dominance in the Mediterranean. This victory eliminated a major Christian stronghold in the Eastern Mediterranean.

name: Oromo migrations
description: Successive luba-led Oromo gadaa expansions described in Bahrey's Zenahu la Galla, transforming the political geography of the Horn after the Gragn wars.

name: German Peasants' War
description: A massive peasant uprising against nobility and clergy was brutally crushed, killing hundreds of thousands. Though inspired by Lutheran reformation ideas, the movement was ultimately crushed by nobles and princes.

name: Spanish Conquest of Guatemala
description: Spanish conquest of Guatemala led by Pedro de Alvarado. Vicious campaigns against K'iche' and other Maya kingdoms, with Spanish aided by indigenous allies.

name: Battle of Pavia
description: The Spanish victory over France that captured King Francis I and shifted the balance in Italian conflicts.

name: Battle of Mohács
description: Ottoman Sultan Suleiman defeated Hungarian forces, beginning Ottoman conquest of Hungary and establishing Ottoman dominance in the Balkans. This victory marked the beginning of Ottoman expansion into Central Europe.

name: Battle of Sunda Kelapa
description: Fatahillah's 1527 victory renamed Sunda Kelapa to Jayakarta.

name: Mughal Expansion in India
description: The Mughal Empire expanded across much of India under Akbar and his successors, creating one of history's largest and wealthiest empires. Mughal rule transformed Indian culture, administration, and religion for centuries.
hook: Mughal emperors conquered the Indian subcontinent, creating history's third-largest empire at its peak.
narrative: Babur, a Central Asian adventurer, invaded northern India (1526) and defeated the Delhi Sultanate at Panipat. His descendants, especially Akbar (r. 1556-1605), expanded the empire to encompass much of the Indian subcontinent. Akbar's military innovations combined Indian war elephants with Central Asian cavalry and firearms. Key campaigns included the conquest of Gujarat, Bengal, and Malwa. Akbar's tolerance toward Hindu subjects and administrative reforms (land surveys, bureaucratic centralization) created a stable empire. His successors, particularly Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb, expanded further, though Aurangzeb's religious policies sparked Hindu resistance. By 1605, the Mughal Empire was the world's second-largest by population.
significance: Mughal rule created a cosmopolitan empire that blended Islamic and Hindu cultures, producing unique Indo-Islamic art and architecture (Taj Mahal). The empire's wealth and stability attracted European traders. Mughal administrative practices influenced British colonial governance. However, Aurangzeb's religious intolerance weakened the empire, contributing to its decline in the 18th century. The Mughal legacy shaped Indian civilization and remains central to Indian historical identity.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Spanish Conquest of Yucatán
description: Protracted Spanish conquest of Yucatán under Francisco de Montejo. Maya resistance was fierce and prolonged, with final subjugation taking nearly 20 years of hard fighting.

name: Sack of Mombasa (1528)
description: Nuno da Cunha's second Portuguese sack of Mombasa.

name: Battle of Shimbra Kure
description: Imam Ahmad Gragn's first decisive victory over Emperor Dawit II opened Ethiopia to Adal conquest.

name: Inca Civil War (Huáscar vs Atahualpa)
description: Succession war between half-brothers Huáscar and Atahualpa following Huayna Capac's death. Atahualpa's victory divided and weakened the empire, critically enabling Spanish conquest within years.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Inca Civil War (Huáscar vs Atahualpa)

hook: Succession dispute between Inca brothers devastated the empire just before Spanish conquest (1525-1532).
narrative: Following Huayna Capac's death (1525), his sons Huáscar and Atahualpa disputed imperial succession. Military conflict erupted between Huáscar (controlling Cusco) and Atahualpa (controlling northern territories). Atahualpa's forces, better positioned militarily, defeated Huáscar. The civil war lasted approximately seven years. Atahualpa's victory came just as Spanish forces arrived.
significance: The Inca succession war devastated imperial unity and military capacity just as Spanish conquered. Atahualpa's military preoccupation enabled Spanish recruitment of anti-Atahualpa factions.

name: Ethiopian-Adal War
description: 30-year conflict between Christian Ethiopia and Muslim Adal sultanate for regional dominance.

name: Ottoman-Austro-Hungarian Wars
description: 170-year conflict between Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian empires.

name: French Expansion in Americas
description: French traders and colonists established a vast North American empire centered on the St. Lawrence River and Mississippi River systems, though ultimately defeated by the British. French colonial efforts created lasting cultural impacts in Canada and Louisiana.

name: Battle of Amba Sel
description: Gragn's victory at Amba Sel scattered the last large Ethiopian field army and led to the looting of Lalibela and Aksum.

name: Nupe Wars
description: Long arc of Nupe wars from Tsoede's foundation through Oyo invasions, internal succession wars, the Fulani jihad, and British conquest of Bida.

name: Ottoman-Safavid Wars (1532-1555)
description: Series of conflicts between Ottoman and Safavid Persian empires for control of Mesopotamia and the Caucasus, establishing dividing lines that persist today.

name: Spanish Conquest of Peru
description: Francisco Pizarro conquered the vast Inca Empire with a small force, extracting enormous wealth and establishing Spanish colonial rule. The conquest, combined with disease, devastated Andean indigenous populations.

casualtyRange.source: Wikipedia: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire
casualtyRange.notes: Conquest 1532-1572. Combat + disease/enslavement aftermath. Inca population fell ~80%.

hook: Francisco Pizarro's soldiers toppled the Inca Empire and established Spanish rule over vast Andean territories.
narrative: In 1532, Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro arrived in Peru with about 170 men. The Inca Empire, the world's largest pre-Columbian state, was fractured by civil war between the brothers Huascar and Atahualpa. Pizarro exploited divisions by allying with indigenous groups. At Cajamarca (1532), Pizarro captured Atahualpa through treachery and ransomed him for gold and silver; Atahualpa was subsequently executed. Pizarro's forces then marched on Cusco, the capital, though resistance continued under Manco Inca (1536-1572). Spanish reinforcements and disease gradually overwhelmed Inca resistance. By 1572, Spanish colonial rule was firmly established; the last Inca stronghold fell.
significance: The conquest of Peru provided Spain with vast wealth (silver from Potosí mines) and an empire spanning South America. The conquest devastated indigenous populations through warfare, enslavement, and disease (estimated 1-10 million deaths). The Spanish imposed Christianity and feudal labor systems (encomienda). The conquest established Spain as the dominant European power and financed its wars in Europe for centuries.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Spanish Conquest of the Inca Empire
description: Francisco Pizarro's conquest of the Inca Empire, one of history's most consequential conquests, establishing Spanish colonial rule in South America.
hook: Francisco Pizarro's conquistadors toppled the Inca Empire through treachery, disease, and superior military tactics.
narrative: The Spanish Conquest of the Inca Empire (1532-1572) involved Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro and a force of about 170 men conquering a vast empire of 10 million people. Pizarro exploited the Inca civil war between brothers Huascar and Atahualpa. At Cajamarca (1532), Pizarro captured Atahualpa through a deceptive ambush and subsequently executed him despite receiving a room full of gold as ransom. Spanish forces, equipped with firearms, horses, and steel weapons, overwhelmed Inca armies initially. However, Spanish consolidation took decades; resistance continued under Manco Inca (1536-1572) and his descendants. Smallpox, introduced by Europeans, devastated the Inca population. By 1572, the last Inca stronghold fell.
significance: The Spanish Conquest of the Inca Empire provided Spain with vast wealth (silver from Potosí mines, estimated at 16,000 tons by the 18th century) that financed Spanish power for centuries. The conquest decimated indigenous populations through warfare, enslavement, and disease (estimated 10 million deaths). The conquest imposed Christianity, Spanish language, and feudal labor systems (encomienda and later hacienda) on the Inca peoples. The conquest fundamentally transformed South America's political, cultural, and economic structure. Peru's indigenous heritage, while suppressed, persisted and influenced post-colonial identity.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Lê-Mạc Wars
description: Vietnamese civil conflict between Lê and Mạc dynasties competing for legitimacy and control, contributing to fragmentation of Vietnamese state.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Baghdad
description: Ottoman forces conquered Baghdad from the Safavids, establishing Ottoman control over Iraq for 400 years. This victory secured Ottoman dominance of Mesopotamian territory and resources.

name: Dano-Swedish Wars
description: The series of wars between Denmark and Sweden for control of the Baltic region.

name: Tunis Expedition (1535)
description: Charles V's amphibious capture of Tunis and La Goletta from Hayreddin Barbarossa, restoring the Hafsid Muley Hassan as vassal.

name: Toungoo–Hanthawaddy War
description: Tabinshwehti's conquest of Mon Pegu founded the First Toungoo Empire.

name: Araucanian War
description: Nearly 300-year conflict between Spanish colonial forces and the Mapuche people of Chile, one of the longest indigenous resistance movements.

name: Arauco War
description: The longest indigenous resistance in the Americas. Mapuche successfully resisted Spanish conquest for 282 years, maintaining independence in southern Chile until Chilean independence.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Second Venetian-Ottoman War
description: Another Ottoman victory against Venice, further establishing Ottoman naval dominance in the Mediterranean. Venice ceded more Greek territories to Ottoman control.

name: Kaabu Empire Wars
description: Mandinka empire of Kaabu's wars from independence from Mali to its destruction at Kansala.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Yemen
description: Ottoman forces conquered Yemen, establishing Ottoman control over the Red Sea and Indian Ocean approaches. Ottoman rule of Yemen lasted until the 20th century.

name: Mixtón War
description: Rebellion of Mixtón and neighboring peoples in northern Mexico against Spanish colonial rule. Spanish response was brutal; this conflict delayed further Spanish expansion northward.

name: Algiers Expedition (1541)
description: Charles V's disastrous amphibious expedition against Hayreddin Barbarossa's Algiers, wrecked by storm.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Budapest
description: Ottoman forces captured Budapest from Hungary, establishing Ottoman control of Central Hungary. This conquest lasted until the Great Turkish War in the late 17th century.

name: Battle of Wofla
description: Adal-Ottoman forces defeated and captured Cristovão da Gama, who was executed by Imam Ahmad.

name: Battle of Wayna Daga
description: Emperor Gelawdewos and the Portuguese survivors killed Imam Ahmad Gragn in battle, breaking Adal's invasion of Ethiopia.

name: Toungoo–Mrauk-U War (1545–47)
description: Tabinshwehti's failed siege of Mrauk-U.

name: Schmalkaldic War
description: Emperor Charles V defeated the Protestant Schmalkaldic League in a military campaign that temporarily crushed German Protestant resistance. However, the religious conflict remained unresolved and escalated after this war.
hook: 1546-1547 conflict between Catholic Emperor and Protestant German princes solidified Reformation divisions.
narrative: The Schmalkaldic League, an alliance of Protestant German princes, resisted Holy Roman Emperor Charles V's attempt to restore Catholic dominance. The war pitted Protestant military forces against imperial armies. The Protestant defeat at Mühlberg (1547) ended the war. However, the subsequent Peace of Augsburg (1555) established the principle of cuius regio, eius religio—allowing territorial rulers to determine their lands' religious character. The Schmalkaldic conflict demonstrated that religious division could not be resolved militarily.
significance: The Schmalkaldic War's outcome institutionalized Protestant-Catholic coexistence in Germany. The conflict presaged the Thirty Years' War's religious dimension. The peace established precedents for religious toleration.

name: Burmese–Siamese War (1547–1549)
description: Tabinshwehti's siege of Ayutthaya failed, but Burma seized Upper Tenasserim.

name: Burmese–Siamese wars
description: A series of armed conflicts between the Burmese Toungoo/Konbaung empires and the Siamese Ayutthaya/Thonburi/Rattanakosin kingdoms, fought intermittently from 1547 to 1855. See per-war entries.
hook: Centuries of conflicts between Burma and Siam determined control of Southeast Asian territory and regional dominance.
narrative: The Burmese-Siamese Wars (16th-19th centuries) were a series of conflicts between the Burmese and Siamese kingdoms for regional dominance. Major wars included the Burmese conquest of Siam under King Thaungyin (1550s-1560s), subsequent Siamese-Burmese conflicts (1600s), and the major war of 1824-1826. Burmese forces, particularly under King Alaungpaya (18th century), defeated Siam multiple times. The conflicts demonstrated the military superiority of Burmese cavalry and warfare tactics. The wars resulted in territorial changes, with Burma gaining influence over Siamese territories and populations. By the 19th century, both nations had become subordinated to British colonial rule (Burma directly; Siam maintained nominal independence).
significance: The Burmese-Siamese Wars demonstrated the power balance in Southeast Asia and established Burma as a major regional power until British colonization. The wars' outcome influenced territorial boundaries and the ethnic composition of modern Burma and Thailand. The conflicts influenced Southeast Asian politics and the historical narratives of both nations. The wars' legacy contributed to modern Thai-Myanmar tensions and territorial disputes. The conflicts demonstrated the military effectiveness of Southeast Asian kingdoms before European colonization.

name: Wolof Civil Wars (Battle of Danki)
description: Cayor and Baol's breakaway wars that destroyed the Jolof Empire's hegemony over Senegal.

name: Capture of Mahdia (1550)
description: Spanish-Knights of Malta capture of the Ottoman corsair base of Mahdia from Turgut Reis.

name: Jiajing Mongol Raids
description: Altan Khan's raids on Ming borders, culminating in peace treaty.

name: Chichimeca War
description: Longest and most difficult Spanish conquest-era conflict in northern Mexico. Chichimeca resistance on the Bajío frontier lasted 40 years despite superior Spanish forces.

name: Otomo-Shimazu Conflicts
description: Rival clans fighting for control of Kyushu island.

name: Loango Expansion
description: Period in which the Vili kingdom of Loango extended its commercial empire along the north Congo coast, projecting power into Kakongo, Ngoyo and Mayombe.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Tripoli
description: Ottoman forces conquered Tripoli from the Knights of Malta, establishing Ottoman control over North Africa. This victory secured Ottoman dominance of Mediterranean trade routes.

name: Battle of Tucapel
description: Mapuche victory under Lautaro against Spanish governor Pedro de Valdivia. This battle galvanized indigenous resistance in the Arauco region.

name: Takeda-Uesugi Conflicts
description: Famous daimyo conflicts over Shinano province, including Kawanakajima battles.

name: Treaty of Amasya - Ottoman-Safavid Peace
description: A peace treaty established a relatively stable border between the Ottoman and Safavid empires. The treaty established the modern border between Turkey and Iran.

name: Mori-Takeda Conflicts
description: Extended conflicts between Mori and Takeda clans for western control.

name: Ottoman-Safavid Wars in Caucasus
description: Ottoman and Safavid forces competed for control of the Caucasus, with both empires making territorial gains at different periods. The region became a contested borderland between the empires.

name: Kongo-Ndongo War of 1556
description: Defeat of Kongo forces by the Ngola of Ndongo that effectively ended Kongo's claim to suzerainty south of the Dande River.

name: Ottoman–Ethiopian War (1557–1589)
description: Özdemir Pasha's seizure of Massawa, Arqiqo and Debarwa created the Habesh Eyalet; Sarsa Dengel finally drove the Ottomans back to the coast at Addi Qaro.

name: Burmese–Lao War (1558–1563)
description: Bayinnaung's repeated campaigns subdued Lan Xang's Setthathirath.

name: Livonian War
description: 25-year war ending Livonian Order dominance and reshaping Baltic.

name: Battle of Hazalo
description: Emperor Gelawdewos was killed in battle against Nur ibn Mujahid of Harar at Hazalo.

name: Battle of Djerba
description: Ottoman naval forces decisively defeated a Christian coalition fleet, securing Ottoman naval supremacy in the Mediterranean. This victory prevented a Christian counter-offensive in North Africa.

name: French Wars of Religion
description: A series of eight civil wars between Catholics and Protestant Huguenots devastated France for 36 years. The wars ended with the Edict of Nantes, establishing religious toleration but leaving France weakened.
hook: Huguenot and Catholic factions tore France apart in religious civil wars that killed hundreds of thousands.
narrative: After the Protestant Reformation, France's Calvinist Huguenots (about 10% of the population by 1560) clashed with Catholic dominance. Between 1562 and 1598, eight major wars erupted, often triggered by royal succession disputes and noble family rivalries. The massacre of Protestant Huguenots on St. Bartholomew's Day (August 1572) killed 10,000-30,000 and shocked Protestant Europe. Battles raged from Paris to the provinces; foreign powers (Spain, England, Rome) supported factions. The wars devastated the French economy and population. Henry of Navarre (a Huguenot) emerged as the strongest warlord and converted to Catholicism to gain the throne as Henry IV (1589). The Edict of Nantes (1598) granted Huguenots religious freedom and political rights.
significance: The Wars of Religion killed 2-3 million people and revealed the fragility of religious pluralism in early modern states. They established the principle of religious toleration (limited) in European politics. Henry IV's pragmatic conversion and the Edict of Nantes created a model for managing religious diversity. The wars' devastation contributed to France's decline relative to Spain in the late 16th century.

sources.label: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: French Wars of Religion - Huguenot Conflicts
description: Eight civil wars between Catholics and Huguenots devastated France, ending with the Edict of Nantes granting religious tolerance. The wars weakened French power and enabled other European states to rise.
hook: Religious violence between Catholic and Reformed faiths triggered nearly 40 years of French civil warfare.
narrative: The Wars of Religion (1562-1598) stemmed from the rise of French Protestantism and noble family rivalries. The Guise family championed Catholicism; the Bourbon and Montmorency families supported Huguenot rights. The massacre of Protestants at Wassy (1562) sparked the First War. Eight wars followed, with armies clashing in numerous campaigns (Dreux, Moncontour, Coutras). The St. Bartholomew's massacre (1572) attempted to decapitate the Huguenot leadership but instead solidified Protestant resistance. Naval warfare in the Atlantic complemented land campaigns. Henry of Navarre's survival and military victories made him indispensable; his conversion and subsequent reign as Henry IV established the Bourbon dynasty and the Edict of Nantes.
significance: The Wars of Religion killed 2-3 million people and devastated France's economy and population. They established religious toleration as a principle of governance (via the Edict of Nantes). The Bourbon dynasty's rise reshaped European power dynamics. The wars demonstrated how religious schism could fracture states and the necessity of political compromise.

sources.label: Wikipedia: French Wars of Religion - Huguenot Conflicts
Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Rajput-Mughal Wars
description: Mughal campaigns against independent Rajput kingdoms.
hook: Mughal conquest of Rajput kingdoms integrated northwestern India into Mughal administrative system.
narrative: Mughal emperors, particularly Akbar, conducted military campaigns against independent Rajput kingdoms. Rajput resistance and valor became legendary, but Mughal military superiority and diplomatic alliances gradually incorporated Rajput territories. Many Rajput kingdoms became Mughal vassal states.
significance: Rajput conquest established Mughal control over northwestern India. Rajput military traditions were integrated into Mughal military organization.

name: Burmese–Siamese War (1563–1564)
description: War over the White Elephants forced Ayutthaya to acknowledge Toungoo overlordship.

name: Idris Alooma's Wars
description: Mai Idris Alooma's musket-equipped campaigns that restored Bornu hegemony over Kanem and the Lake Chad basin.

name: Battle of Talikota
description: The Deccan sultanates' victory that ended Vijayanagara dominance and marked decline of the Hindu empire.
hook: 1565 battle between Vijayanagara Empire and Deccan sultanates ended Hindu hegemony in South India.
narrative: The Deccan sultanates (Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, Golconda) allied against Vijayanagara in 1565. The alliance decisively defeated Vijayanagara forces at Talikota. The victory destroyed Vijayanagara military dominance.
significance: Talikota ended Vijayanagara as a major power. The victory enabled Islamic sultanate dominance in South India.

name: Siege of Malta (1565)
description: Ottoman siege of Malta launched from North African bases, repelled by the Knights of St. John under La Valette.

name: Spanish colonization of the Philippines
description: Legazpi's expedition seized Cebu and Manila, founding Spanish rule.

name: Spanish Conquest of the Philippines
description: Spanish forces under Miguel López de Legazpi conquered the Philippine Islands, establishing Spanish colonial rule that would last over 300 years. The conquest involved subduing Muslim sultanates and indigenous resistance movements.

name: Spanish–Moro conflict
description: 333-year intermittent warfare between Spain and the southern Muslim sultanates.

name: Siege of Malacca (1568)
description: Sultan Alauddin al-Kahar's failed Acehnese siege of Portuguese Malacca.

name: Burmese–Siamese War (1568–1569)
description: Bayinnaung's second siege captured Ayutthaya on 2 August 1569.

name: Jaga Invasion of Kongo
description: Devastating invasion by the Jaga that drove King Alvaro I from Mbanza Kongo and was reversed only by a Portuguese expeditionary force under Francisco de Gouveia Sottomaior in 1574.

name: Portuguese-Mutapa War (1568-1575)
description: Francisco Barreto's failed Portuguese expedition up the Zambezi to seize the gold mines of Mutapa, recounted by Beach and Newitt as the opening Portuguese intervention.

name: Eighty Years' War
description: 80-year conflict establishing Dutch independence from Spain.

name: Eighty Years' War - Revolt of the Netherlands
description: The Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule initiated an 80-year conflict that resulted in Dutch independence and the rise of the Dutch as a major naval and commercial power. This struggle profoundly shaped European history and colonialism.
hook: Dutch rebels fought Spanish rule for 80 years, establishing an independent Dutch republic and a major sea power.
narrative: The Eighty Years' War (1568-1648) began as a revolt of the Dutch Netherlands against Spanish Habsburg rule. The Dutch, motivated by religious (Calvinist Protestant) and economic grievances, rebelled under leaders like William of Orange. The conflict combined land warfare in the Low Countries with naval conflicts across the Atlantic and Mediterranean. The Dutch developed superior naval technology and tactics, enabling them to project power globally. The Spanish Army of Flanders was one of Europe's finest armies, but Dutch resilience and resourcefulness enabled the Northern Netherlands to eventually establish independence. The Peace of Westphalia (1648) recognized Dutch independence, making the Dutch Republic a sovereign nation.
significance: The Eighty Years' War resulted in the establishment of the Dutch Republic, a powerful European nation and major sea power. Dutch victory demonstrated that sustained resistance could overthrow established empires. The war's outcome established Protestantism in northern Europe and enabled Dutch religious pluralism. Dutch naval and commercial dominance in the 17th century was a direct consequence of their military victory. The war reshaped European power dynamics and established the Netherlands as a major colonial power.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Eighty Years' War - Revolt of the Netherlands
Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Ayutthaya-Toungoo Conflicts
description: Burma captured and sacked Ayutthaya, Siam's capital, but failed to maintain control.
hook: Conflicts between Ayutthaya Kingdom and Toungoo Burma for mainland Southeast Asian hegemony.
narrative: Toungoo, a rising Burmese power, clashed militarily with Ayutthaya for regional dominance. The conflicts involved campaigns and tributary disputes. Ayutthaya's superior resources and organization generally prevailed.
significance: Ayutthaya-Toungoo conflicts maintained Thai dominance while demonstrating Burmese military recovery.

name: Azai-Oda Conflicts
description: Oda Nobunaga's campaign against Azai clan.

name: Cyprus War (Ottoman-Venetian)
description: Ottoman conquest of Cyprus from Venice, establishing Ottoman control of eastern Mediterranean.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Cyprus
description: Ottoman forces conquered Cyprus from Venice despite Christian naval victory at Lepanto, establishing Ottoman control of the eastern Mediterranean. Cyprus remained Ottoman for over 300 years.

name: Third Venetian-Ottoman War
description: Ottoman forces conquered Cyprus from Venice, though the Holy League achieved a naval victory at Lepanto. Despite Lepanto, Ottoman naval power recovered and Venice had to cede Cyprus.

name: Kano–Katsina Wars
description: Two centuries of intermittent war between the rival Hausa city-states of Kano and Katsina over trade routes and tribute.

name: Battle of Lepanto
description: The Holy League Christian fleet achieved a decisive naval victory against the Ottoman Navy, though it was not strategically conclusive. This battle became symbolic of Christian resistance to Ottoman expansion despite Ottoman recovery afterward.

name: Battle of Massapa
description: Engagement during the Barreto expedition against the Mongas, fought near the Portuguese feira of Massapa on the Mutapa frontier.

name: St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre
description: Massacre of Huguenots (French Protestants) in Paris.

name: Battle of Manila (1574)
description: Chinese warlord Limahong's failed assault on Spanish Manila.

name: Conquest of Tunis (1574)
description: Sinan Pasha's Ottoman conquest ending Hafsid rule and the Spanish presidio at La Goletta, completing Ottoman control of the Maghreb.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Tunis
description: Ottoman forces conquered Tunis from Spanish and local rulers, establishing Ottoman control over North Africa. This victory secured Ottoman dominance of the western Mediterranean.

name: Portuguese Conquest of Angola
description: Century-long Portuguese campaign of conquest beginning with Paulo Dias de Novais's 1575 expedition and culminating with the destruction of Kongo at Mbwila and Soyo at Kitombo.

name: Mughal Conquest of Bengal
description: Mughal forces conquered Bengal from the Bengal Sultanate, expanding Mughal control over eastern India. Bengal became one of the Mughal Empire's wealthiest provinces.

name: Queen Amina's Conquests
description: Queen Amina of Zazzau's wars expanding Zaria's reach south to the Niger and east into Kano's sphere.

name: Battle of Addi Qaro
description: Emperor Sarsa Dengel destroyed the Ottoman-supported Bahr Negash Yeshaq at Addi Qaro, restoring Ethiopian control of the highlands.

name: Battle of Alcacer Quibir (Battle of the Three Kings)
description: Catastrophic Portuguese defeat in which King Sebastian I died, triggering the Iberian Union and consolidating Saadi power.

name: Castilian War
description: Spanish expedition under De Sande briefly captured Brunei before withdrawal.

name: Ottoman-Safavid Wars (1578-1590)
description: Ottoman campaigns in Azerbaijan and Caucasus against Safavid Persia, extending Ottoman influence eastward.

name: Spanish-Portuguese Union Wars
description: Philip II of Spain conquered Portugal, uniting the Iberian peninsula for 60 years. Portuguese independence was restored after a rebellion in 1640.

name: Russian Conquest of Siberia
description: Gradual Cossack expansion across Siberia, establishing Russian control over vast territories and subjugating indigenous populations.

name: Russian Expansion into Siberia
description: Russian Cossacks and state forces conquered vast Siberian territories in the largest territorial expansion of any state in this period. This conquest incorporated millions of square kilometers and indigenous peoples into the Russian empire.

name: Battle of Massangano
description: Portuguese victory over Ndongo forces on the Kwanza River that secured the inland presidio of Massangano as the base for further conquest.

name: Burmese–Siamese War (1584–1593)
description: Naresuan's rebellion climaxed in the 1593 elephant duel at Nong Sarai.

name: Mir Ali Bey's expeditions
description: Portuguese fleet trapped Mir Ali Bey's Ottoman corsair squadron at Mombasa while the cannibal Zimba sacked the city from the landward side.

name: Anglo-Spanish War (1585-1604)
description: Conflict ending Spanish naval supremacy with English victory.

name: Anglo-Spanish War - Spanish Armada
description: Spanish King Philip II's attempt to invade England with the Spanish Armada was defeated by English forces and storms, establishing English naval supremacy. This victory marked England's emergence as a major naval power.

name: Dutch-Spanish Wars
description: Major conflict establishing Dutch independence.

name: English-Spanish Colonial Wars
description: English privateers and naval forces challenged Spanish colonial dominance in the Americas, capturing colonies and disrupting Spanish treasure fleets. English success enabled English colonial expansion in the Caribbean.

name: Luba Empire Expansion under Kalala Ilunga
description: Conquests traditionally credited to Kalala Ilunga that built the Luba kingdom around the Upemba lakes by overthrowing Nkongolo Mwamba.

name: English Colonial Expansion in Americas
description: English colonists established settlements in North America and the Caribbean, gradually displacing indigenous peoples and competing with Spain and France. English colonial success laid the foundation for future American dominance.
hook: English colonization of North America dispossessed indigenous peoples and created the foundation for a new nation.
narrative: English colonial expansion in North America (1607-1776) began with the Virginia Company's settlement at Jamestown (1607). Subsequent English colonies—Massachusetts, Connecticut, New York, the Carolinas—expanded along the Atlantic coast. English settlers used enslaved African labor and dispossessed indigenous peoples. Key conflicts included the Powhatan Confederacy Wars, King Philip's War (1675), and the Pueblo Revolt (1680). English expansion was driven by mercantilism, religious freedom (particularly Puritanism), and land acquisition. The colonies developed distinct societies: southern plantation economies dependent on slavery and northern commerce-based economies.
significance: English colonial expansion in North America created thirteen colonies that would become the United States. The expansion resulted in the near-complete dispossession of indigenous peoples and the establishment of plantation slavery as an economic system. The colonies' experience shaped American political philosophy, particularly regarding representation and individual rights. The colonial period established patterns of racial slavery that would define American history. The colonies' growth eventually challenged British imperial control, leading to the American Revolution.

sources.label: Wikipedia: English Colonial Expansion in Americas
Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Tondo Conspiracy
description: Failed plot by Tagalog datus and Bornean allies against Spanish rule.

name: Zimba Raids
description: Northward sweep of the Zimba war-bands from the Lower Zambezi up the Swahili coast, sacking Kilwa and besieging Mombasa.

name: Battle of the Lukala
